name: Macrophage
summary: A large, long-lived phagocyte found in nearly every tissue, often with swallowed debris inside. Resident macrophages clear dead cells and microbes, and each organ has its own type, such as Kupffer cells in the liver. In infection they raise the alarm with cytokines and, once activated by T cells, kill microbes more effectively.
functions: Clears dying cells and debris every day without raising an alarm (efferocytosis); this housekeeping is its commonest job.

Engulfs microbes through receptors for microbial patterns, antibody and complement, and kills them in its lysosomes with enzymes and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Some microbes, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, survive inside macrophages.
Raises the alarm: it releases TNF, IL-1β, IL-6 and chemokines such as CCL2 (and CXCL8 in humans) that call in neutrophils and monocytes and start inflammation.
Is activated further by IFN-γ from Th1 cells and NK cells, which makes it a stronger killer, or by IL-4 and IL-13 from Th2 cells, which turns it toward repair and anti-parasite work.
Debated: the "M1" and "M2" labels for these two states. In tissue, macrophages show a spectrum of states, and the labels come largely from cells treated in culture.

Passes the immune response on: it shows peptides on MHC class II to effector CD4 T cells, and in lymph nodes subcapsular sinus macrophages catch particles and viruses in the lymph and hand them to B cells, while medullary macrophages clear the lymph before it leaves.
In germinal centres, tingible body macrophages engulf the many B cells that die after failing selection, which keeps the dead cells from building up.

Drives repair as well as defence: after engulfing dying neutrophils it switches to releasing growth factors and anti-inflammatory signals. Chronic activation can instead build granulomas or scar tissue.

Many tissue macrophages are not simply monocyte-derived. Fate-mapping in mice shows that microglia, Kupffer cells and alveolar macrophages arise before birth and renew themselves, whereas gut macrophages are replaced from blood monocytes. Human evidence is thinner.
abundance: Not found in blood; monocytes are their blood precursors. Numbers vary widely by organ: macrophages are among the most common immune cells in the liver, lung, spleen and gut wall. Exact human counts are hard to give because the cells must be taken from tissue, and most figures come from mice.
